entries.reason: written, and in the object of its own measured release: xmake l tools/cache-index/first-rung.lua GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot answers 7.0, so the class is in GCSnapshots7.m beside GCGamepadSnapshot rather than in an object of its own. What a snapshot is, is the header's own - a profile of the extended game's elements that holds the values it was saved from and answers them again - so it holds the data and pushes it through the same accessors a live game uses, and the layout it reads is the packed structure GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot.h:41-78 documents

entries.reason: written, and the wall that stopped it is gone. The SDK declares -saveSnapshot at 7.0 (GCExtendedGamepad.h:65) returning GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot, and xmake l tools/cache-index/first-rung.lua places that class at 7.0 as well - not at the 9.0 the SDK header API_AVAILABLE says, which is what the earlier refusal was built on. So the class and the method are on one rung and in one object, GCSnapshots7.m, and a method IMP's objc-class-ref for its return type has its class in the same object. Measured on that object with nm -u: before the method it named GCExtendedGamepad, GCGamepad, NSData, NSDictionary and NSNumber; after, those same five - and the object itself defines GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot, so the reference resolves here and the dylib links. The reading is the extended game's own elements and the layout is the structure GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot.h:41-78 documents
entries.effect: the extended game's own values as data: a GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot holding the 63-byte GCExtendedGamepadSnapshotData with its version 0x0101 and size in the first four bytes. With no controller attached every value is zero, the data is 0101 3f00 followed by zeros, and byte 60 - supportsClickableThumbsticks - is 01 because the extended profile carries both thumbstick buttons, which is what the host writes for a controller nothing has touched. The caller can read the snapshot back with -initWithSnapshotData: and every element answers the value the data holds
entries.source: the header of iOS 16.4 (GCExtendedGamepad.h:65 the method, GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot.h:24-31 the class and its two initialisers, :41-78 the structure) and xmake l tools/cache-index/first-rung.lua GCExtendedGamepadSnapshot, which answers 7.0; the link wall measured with nm -u on the port's own GCSnapshots7.o; and this Mac's own GameController as the oracle, where the `snapshot objects` group of tests/backports/host/gamecontroller compares the host's -saveSnapshot over its untouched gamepad against the port's - object against object, 63 bytes beginning 0101 3f00 with byte 60 written 01 on both - and the port-only `snapshot read back` group holds each of three matrices of field values against the host's own NSDataFromGCExtendedGamepadSnapshotData for the same values, byte for byte

entries.reason: written, and in the object of its own measured release. measured_names() answers NONE for a method - it reads classes and C functions off the caches, not Objective-C methods - so the registry's introduced is what places it, and the floor it cannot precede is its own return type: GCMicroGamepadSnapshot first arrives at 10.0.1 (xmake l tools/cache-index/first-rung.lua). The SDK header says API_DEPRECATED(..., ios(7.0, 13.0)) on GCMicroGamepad.h:101, and 7.0 is when the deprecation range opens, not when the method became reachable on this ladder. So the method is carried at 10.0.1, beside its snapshot class in GCSnapshots9.m, which is one release in one object. It is the same two steps either way - read the current values into the structure, hand the structure to the encoder - and the encoder is the one CharonGCSnapshot.h holds, which is the layout GCMicroGamepadSnapshot.h:39-52 documents
entries.effect: the micro game's values as data: a GCMicroGamepadSnapshot holding the 20-byte GCMicroGamepadSnapshotData with its version 0x0100 and size in the first four bytes. With no controller attached every value is zero and the data is 0001 1400 followed by zeros
entries.source: the header of iOS 16.4; the bytes are held against the host's own NSDataFromGCMicroGamepadSnapshotData by the `snapshot objects` group of tests/backports/host/gamecontroller over a matrix of values - a dpadX of -0.5 in the port's own bytes against the host encoder's is what found the direction pad being read as if it were an axis
